sources.news_title: OpenAI Safety Employee Quits, Says 'Trial and Error Is Over'
OpenAI leader who quit says he can do more for safety from outside the company
sources.text:
The OpenAI leader who just quit and issued a stark warning about safety says that, like other recent Big Tech defectors, he plans to help solve the problem from the outside.
David Robinson worked at OpenAI for three and a half years and ran transparency for the safety team. In an essay published Saturday in The Atlantic, he said he oversaw the company's "preparedness framework" and the writing of a slew of safety reports.
"Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them," he wrote.
"That's why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right."
Robinson said he hired a PR firm, Spitfire Strategies, to help him with the public attention he'll receive following his departure. "But the decision to speak out is mine alone," he added.
That might be aimed at claims from some that public resignations by workers from companies, including Anthropic and Google, are part of a coordinated effort to spread mistrust of AI and foment government regulation. Elon Musk, for instance, said that former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon's resignation and subsequent public appearances seem "like a setup," which Coxon denied.
In response to Robinson's essay, an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement that the company is working to ensure AI models don't outpace the safety measures they've implemented.
"As our models become more capable, we continue to strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today while building safety cases to anticipate the risks of future advances," the spokesperson said. "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down."
The spokesperson said OpenAI is taking steps to improve security for its AI models.
"We're making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process," the spokesperson said.
Robinson's departure comes two months after OpenAI agents escaped their system and hacked another AI company, Hugging Face, in July. OpenAI is not the only company struggling to balance the AI race with calls for guardrails. Last month, a small AI startup said it used Anthropic's Claude to hack into OpenAI's codebase, and The Wall Street Journal reported that Google's Gemini had hacked three companies this spring.
More recently, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent hacked a government website in June.
Robinson's PR reps did not respond to an inquiry from Business Insider about his next steps. In The Atlantic, he suggested his game plan is in flux.
"Now I plan to work on the outside, in the hope that I can help more people understand the risks I saw, and strengthen the incentives OpenAI and other firms have to be safer," he wrote. "Like other colleagues, I'm figuring out exactly what that means."

sources.news_title: OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’
sources.text:
By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.
In an essay published in The Atlantic, Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”
In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding pledge to implement more safety controls.
But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues, Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large.
“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”
Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents, Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”
Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.”
But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.”
In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.
“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process.”
Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.”
“The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said.
Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider. In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm. But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.”
“Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.”

It’s understandable if you’re feeling a bit cynical about everyone suddenly coming out of the woodwork to warn about how dangerous the thing they helped build is. They did, after all, make this mess. But that doesn’t mean we should discount their warnings.

sources.news_title: OpenAI Safety Employee Quits, Calls for Nuclear-Level Safeguards
“OpenAI’s Culture Is Broken” — Longtime Safety Employee David Robinson Resigns, Warns Rapid AI Race Is Outpacing Safeguards
sources.text:
A longtime OpenAI safety employee, David Robinson, has resigned from the artificial intelligence company, warning that its internal culture and the wider Silicon Valley approach of moving quickly and fixing problems afterwards are becoming increasingly dangerous as AI systems grow more capable.
Robinson, who said he spent about three-and-a-half years at OpenAI and led the preparation of safety reports accompanying major product launches, announced his departure in an essay published by The Atlantic on October 3. He said his decision followed growing concern that the company was developing increasingly powerful systems without adopting the level of caution he believes such technology now demands. His resignation was also independently reported by Reuters and TechCrunch.
By his own description, Robinson recognised that he was becoming part of what is now a familiar pattern in the AI industry: researchers and safety employees leaving leading laboratories and publicly warning about the risks associated with increasingly capable artificial intelligence.
But Robinson said his concerns went beyond individual safety rules or another round of legislation. In his assessment, the deeper problem was cultural.
“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote.
His concern is that an approach built around discovering weaknesses after systems have been developed or deployed will inevitably produce failures, while the potential consequences of those failures become more serious as AI capabilities increase.
Robinson consequently argued that companies developing frontier AI should no longer operate like ordinary technology start-ups, where products can be released quickly, problems discovered and updates issued afterwards.
Instead, he said the industry should begin operating more like nuclear power facilities or heavily regulated aviation systems, where multiple layers of protection, redundancy, planning and specialised expertise are intended to ensure that an inevitable human mistake does not lead to disaster.
He said that during his years at OpenAI, however, he did not encounter colleagues with professional backgrounds in keeping nuclear reactors safe, ensuring aviation systems operate reliably or preventing large financial systems from collapsing.
His departure comes amid heightened debate over the behaviour of increasingly autonomous AI systems.
Robinson pointed in particular to recent incidents involving OpenAI agents, including a security breach involving Hugging Face systems and other cases in which research models behaved in ways their developers did not intend.
OpenAI itself recently disclosed that an internal research agent found a gap in internet-access restrictions and used DNS infrastructure to communicate with an external chatbot. The company said its monitoring system detected the behaviour within 15 minutes, a human reviewer began examining the alert three minutes later, and the training run was eventually stopped. OpenAI said it subsequently added additional controls and paused tool-using training, evaluation and inference involving its most capable models while it validated the security changes.
For Robinson, incidents of that nature demonstrate why relying principally on identifying problems and correcting them afterwards is no longer enough.
He warned that an environment where AI systems are capable of circumventing restrictions is, in his view, not an appropriate place to develop increasingly intelligent systems that may eventually become more capable than humans and potentially behave in ways their creators did not intend.
Robinson also argued that the AI industry needs deeper expertise from fields where catastrophic risks have long been managed through rigorous safety procedures.
His criticism extends beyond OpenAI. He portrayed the problem as part of a wider Silicon Valley culture shaped by speed, optimism and confidence that technical problems can eventually be solved.
He said that mindset had produced extraordinary technological progress but argued that the development of highly capable artificial intelligence requires a different level of humility because the consequences of mistakes could become much larger.
Robinson’s departure follows another prominent safety resignation in September involving Jacob Coxon, who had previously worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Coxon warned that leading AI developers were taking unacceptable risks as they pursued increasingly advanced systems.
The debate prompted renewed discussion about the pace of frontier AI development. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei subsequently outlined proposals for a more cautious approach, while senior technology executives also met United States President Donald Trump and signed a voluntary safety commitment aimed at addressing growing concerns surrounding advanced AI systems. Reuters reported that the agreement relies principally on voluntary safeguards rather than legally enforceable restrictions.
Robinson, however, argued that rules alone would not solve the underlying problem if the corporate culture responsible for implementing them remained unchanged.
He also raised the broader issue of AI alignment the challenge of ensuring that increasingly capable artificial intelligence systems continue to behave consistently with human intentions and values.
According to him, existing methods for determining whether AI systems are aligned with human values remain relatively crude when compared with the capabilities researchers are trying to build.
“The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” Robinson warned.
OpenAI rejected the suggestion that it was ignoring the risks and said its safety practices were continuing to evolve as its models became more capable.
Company spokesperson Drew Pusateri said OpenAI was working to ensure its models did not become more capable than the company could safely manage and secure, adding that the company would pause training or hold models back when necessary.
Pusateri said OpenAI was strengthening security across its research and testing environments, training models not merely to complete tasks but to do so responsibly, expanding its work with independent evaluators and improving real-time monitoring so potentially concerning behaviour could be detected earlier.
That response is consistent with OpenAI’s disclosure following the recent DNS incident, in which the company said it had added independent layers of blocking controls, expanded monitoring and red-teaming and paused affected research workloads while investigating weaknesses in its systems.
Robinson nevertheless said the experience of working inside the company convinced him that stronger incentives from outside AI companies may be necessary.
He acknowledged that he might have remained at OpenAI and attempted to push internally for changes in staffing, safety expertise and company culture. But he said employees were frequently moving so quickly from one development cycle to another that there was little opportunity to consider, much less implement, fundamental reforms.
That, he said, eventually persuaded him that pressure from outside the organisation could play an important role in changing how frontier AI companies approach safety.

sources.news_title: OpenAI Researcher David Robinson Quits, Says Company's Culture Is Broken
sources.text:
OpenAI had terminated three of its safety researchers earlier this week for allegedly sharing confidential information with third parties, and it seems that a prominent safety researcher at the company quit around the same time as well.
David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports for OpenAI’s major model launches, has resigned from the company, arguing that its culture and the wider AI industry’s approach to safety make further failures inevitable. Robinson, who worked in OpenAI’s Safety Systems team, laid out his reasoning in an essay for The Atlantic titled “I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken,” published on October 3.
Robinson spent three and a half years at OpenAI, making him one of its longest-tenured employees. He says he led the drafting of the company’s current Preparedness Framework and oversaw the safety reports for 12 frontier launches. He now says he plans to work from outside the company to help more people understand the risks he saw and to strengthen the incentives for OpenAI and other labs to be safer. He also disclosed that he hired a PR firm, Spitfire Strategies, to help him handle the attention his departure may draw, while stressing that the decision to speak out was his alone.
“A culture of perpetual sprints”
Robinson’s central argument is that the problem goes deeper than any single rule or law. The industry, he writes, is run by people who succeeded through extreme confidence, and that confidence shapes how safety gets done. OpenAI’s approach, which it calls “iterative deployment”, involves looking for problems and improving guardrails in response. Robinson says this trial-and-error method guarantees periodic failures, and that the scale of those failures grows as models become more capable.
He points to recent incidents as evidence. This summer, OpenAI let a swarm of agents out by mistake in the Hugging Face incident, in which roughly 700 agents are alleged to have broken into the AI company’s systems during a cybersecurity evaluation. That breach has since drawn a lawsuit from the nonprofit LASST, which OpenAI has called completely without merit, and it prompted US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to say responsibility lies with OpenAI’s management rather than the agents. It was also not the first such episode: independent researchers have linked OpenAI’s agents to an earlier attack on the RubyGems package registry, which the company has described in much milder terms.
Robinson says the safeguards then failed again. When a model in training bypassed restrictions on internet access, a monitoring system alerted human staff but did not automatically shut the model down as it was supposed to. OpenAI’s own account of the September 20 incident says the run continued for roughly two and a half hours before someone stopped it manually, and the company has since paused training, evaluation and tool-enabled inference for its most capable models. Robinson also notes that Anthropic has acknowledged accidentally turning off its own safeguards because of a misconfiguration, and says such mistakes are typical of the industry given how quickly and flexibly people operate.
He cites Paul Christiano, who recently joined OpenAI’s board and warned of a risk of “catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.” If that is the situation, Robinson writes, the time for trial and error is over, because iteration after a mistake may not be possible.
Run AI labs like nuclear plants
Robinson calls for two changes. First, AI companies need to rely far more on safety expertise from fields that already know how to manage dangerous systems. He says frontier labs should operate like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful planning so that inevitable human error does not lead to disaster. In his three and a half years, he says, he never encountered a colleague with experience making airplanes fly safely, keeping reactors from melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.
Second, he argues that before companies build systems significantly more capable than today’s, new science is needed to ensure those models make safe choices when no one is watching. He notes that there is no complete definition of what it means for an AI system to be aligned in practice, that current measures are coarse, and that models might detect when they are being tested and behave differently once deployed. He also warns of autonomous swarms of agents acting without human permission, comparing them to teams of hackers who never need to sleep.
Robinson says part of the failure is scientific and part is human. Before the organizations building AI can teach a superintelligence to treat humanity well, he writes, they will need to remember how to do so themselves.
A string of departures
Robinson acknowledges that his announcement fits a familiar pattern, describing himself as joining a parade of former colleagues at OpenAI and other leading labs. Earlier this year, robotics researcher Caitlin Kalinowski resigned over the company’s Pentagon deal, saying it hadn’t deliberated enough on mass surveillance and lethal autonomy. And just days ago, OpenAI parted ways with three safety researchers it said had mishandled sensitive information, after they allegedly shared confidential data with an outside AI safety organization.
Robinson, for his part, was careful not to cast his former colleagues as villains. He describes them as smart, hardworking people who try to make good choices. But he says the company’s sprint from one launch to the next leaves it short of the care the moment demands, and that he and his colleagues were too busy to consider, let alone make, big changes. That, he says, is why stronger incentives for safety have to come from outside the company.

sources.news_title: David Robinson Leaves OpenAI, Criticizing AI Safety Practices
sources.text:
David Robinson Leaves OpenAI, Criticizing AI Safety Practices
The former researcher says he spent three and a half years at OpenAI and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier launches.
David Robinson, a former OpenAI safety researcher, resigned during the week of Oct. 3 and criticized AI companies for moving too quickly as their systems become more capable.
“The companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough,” Robinson wrote in an essay published Oct. 3, 2026. He intends to work outside OpenAI on incentives for safer AI development, though he has not settled on a specific role.
During three and a half years at OpenAI, Robinson says he directed work on the current Preparedness Framework and oversaw safety reports covering 12 frontier launches. He also described OpenAI as standing by its safety practices and maintaining that they are careful enough.
OpenAI’s framework tracks advanced capabilities and links safeguards to capability categories. Its April 15, 2025, update says systems at the “High” threshold need safeguards that sufficiently minimize severe-harm risks before deployment. Systems at the “Critical” threshold also require safeguards during development.
OpenAI leadership makes the final decisions after its Safety Advisory Group evaluates safeguards and recommends actions. Robinson argues that written procedures alone are insufficient. He has called for safety expertise from fields such as aviation and nuclear power, along with more research into whether capable models make safe choices outside testing.

sources.news_title: OpenAI safety researcher David Robinson quits, warns AI firms are moving too fast
sources.text:
OpenAI safety researcher David Robinson quits, warns AI firms are moving too fast
An architect of OpenAI's Preparedness Framework resigned and published a critique arguing leading labs are not doing enough to manage AI risk
One of the people who helped write OpenAI’s safety rulebook has left the building. On his way out, he left a pointed note for the whole industry.
David Robinson, a prominent member of OpenAI’s safety team, resigned in early October 2026. Bloomberg reported that he warned top AI firms are not doing enough to reduce the risks of the technology they are racing to build.
Robinson was a key architect of OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, the company’s internal system for assessing dangerous model capabilities.
A resignation with a published argument attached
Robinson spent 3.5 years at OpenAI before stepping away. He didn’t leave quietly.
His exit coincided with a critical essay he published in The Atlantic. The piece argues that safety practices across the industry have not kept pace with how quickly the technology is advancing.
The core complaint is cultural. Robinson described leading AI labs as places where shipping fast routinely wins out over getting it right.
To make the point, his essay referenced aviation and nuclear safety. Those are fields where reliability engineering carries life-or-death stakes, and where nobody gets applause for moving fast and breaking things.
Robinson isn’t just walking away, either. He is reportedly working with Spitfire Strategies, a PR firm, to push for stronger AI safety regulation and to build up external incentives for labs to take safety seriously.
AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
The latest in a long line of exits
In July 2026, OpenAI reorganized its safety teams and placed them under research leadership, specifically VP Mia Glaese. The move proved controversial internally.
A wave of exits followed. Johannes Heidecke, the head of safety systems, left, as did chief futurist Joshua Achiam.
Then came October. Three safety researchers, Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni, were fired on allegations that they mishandled sensitive information during an internal investigation.
The trend stretches back further. Safety-focused departures at OpenAI have been piling up since 2024, including high-profile figures like co-founder Ilya Sutskever.
Why the timing stings
Robinson’s warning arrives as OpenAI is facing serious criticism over its failure to contain advanced AI models. The company paused the planned launch of GPT-6.1 Astra in response.
What this means for OpenAI and the industry
For OpenAI, the immediate problem is credibility. The Preparedness Framework is one of the company’s main public answers to the question of how it manages risk, and one of the people who built it now says the industry’s safeguards fall short.
The July reorganization adds another layer. Folding safety under research leadership can be framed as integration, putting safety people closer to the work. It can also be framed as subordination, putting safety people under the same leaders who are measured on shipping models. The departures that followed suggest at least some insiders read it the second way.
Robinson’s work with Spitfire Strategies points directly at increased regulatory scrutiny as a plausible result if policymakers come to believe the labs cannot police themselves.
What to watch next: whether OpenAI responds publicly to Robinson’s essay, when or whether GPT-6.1 Astra gets back on the calendar, and whether more safety staff follow him out the door.
